title: My family
goal: Talk about your family and jobs, fit in the verb *a avea*, meet the three noun genders through *un* and *o*, and understand why "my mother" in Romanian is literally "mother-the my".
bekal: use all six forms of *a avea* and negate them with *nu am* or *n-am*
choose *un* or *o* according to the noun's gender — masculine, feminine, or neuter
show possession with *meu, mea, tău, ta, lui, ei* after a noun with the definite article

dialogs.title: Dialogue — O fotografie de familie
dialogs.intro: Break time at the office. Ioana is curious about Budi's family in Bandung, and Budi takes out his phone to show her a photo.

lines.speaker: Ioana:
lines.id: Budi, do you have brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Da, am un frate și o soră. Uite o fotografie!
lines.id: Yes, I have a brother and a sister. Look, here's a photo!
lines.literal: yes, I-have a-m brother and a-f sister. look a-f photo!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: That's my mother. She's a teacher.

lines.speaker: Ioana:
lines.id: And him? Is that your father?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes. My father is an engineer.

lines.speaker: Ioana:
lines.text: Și sora ta? Este și ea ingineră?

lines.text: Nu, sora mea este studentă. Fratele meu are o soție și un copil.

lines.text: Nu, avem o familie mică. Am doar un frate. El locuiește în Brașov cu soția lui.
lines.id: No, we have a small family. I only have one brother. He lives in Brașov with his wife.

notes: **Frate and soră don't say older or younger** — just like English *brother* and *sister*. If age matters, add *mai mare* (bigger, older) or *mai mic / mai mică* (smaller, younger): *fratele meu mai mare* = my older brother, *sora mea mai mică* = my younger sister.

**Am un frate și o soră.** *Un* for masculine nouns, *o* for feminine. Both mean "a" and "one" at the same time, so this sentence answers *whether* and *how many* in one go. The plurals *frați* and *surori* (irregular ones) appear without any article; plurals come in unit 5.

**Este mama mea — no pronoun.** The subject is clear from Ioana's question, so *ea* is dropped. Notice also *mama*, not *mamă*: as soon as there's an owner, the noun must take the definite article. That's the point of the second grammar box below.
**Nu am copii.** After a negative, a plural noun stands bare. In conversation you'll more often hear the merged form, *N-am copii* — the *n-am* mentioned in unit 2.
**Soția lui — "his wife".** *Lui* means "his" and *ei* "her"; neither ever changes form, whatever is owned. So *soția lui* = his wife, *soțul ei* = her husband.

grammars.title: A avea, un and o — have a what?
body: *A avea* (to have) is the second most important verb after *a fi*, and later it also becomes the past-tense helper (unit 14) — just like English "I *have* worked". Its forms are short and irregular, so learn them together with the negatives.
after: **Three genders, two articles.** Every Romanian noun is masculine (m), feminine (f), or neuter (n). There are only two indefinite articles: **un** for m and n, **o** for f — *un frate* (m), *un oraș* (n), *o soră* (f). Neuter nouns behave like masculine ones in the singular and like feminine ones in the plural; you'll only feel that in unit 5.

**How to guess the gender.** People follow their natural gender: *tată* and *frate* are masculine, *mamă* and *soră* feminine. For things, look at the ending: **-ă** or **-e** is usually feminine (*o casă, o familie, o fotografie*); a **consonant** or **-u** means masculine or neuter, and for objects it's usually neuter (*un oraș, un birou, un telefon*). This guess is right about nine times out of ten.

**Adjectives follow along.** *O familie mică* but *un oraș mic*; *mare* (big) happens to be the same for both. Notice the position too: adjectives stand **after** the noun, unlike English. Their forms are tidied up in unit 9.

grammars.title: Meu, mea, tău, ta — possession, and why the noun takes the article
body: Unlike English, the Romanian possessive stands **after** the noun — *mama mea* = "mother-the my". And it agrees with the gender and number of the thing owned.
after: **What counts is the thing owned, not the owner.** Budi is a man, but he says *mama mea* because *mamă* is feminine; Ioana is a woman, but she says *fratele meu* because *frate* is masculine. Only *lui, ei,* and *lor* are immune: they really mean "of him / of her / of them", so they don't change.

**The noun must take the definite article**, the little ending glued on behind: *mamă → mama mea*, *soră → sora mea*, *familie → familia mea*, *frate → fratele meu*, *tată → tatăl meu*, *copil → copilul meu*. Think "the mother of mine". *Mamă mea* without the ending sounds as odd as "a mother my". The full rules for the endings come in unit 4; for now, learn the family words as chunks together with *meu* or *mea*.

**What you'll hear on the street.** For their own parents, Romanians often just say *mama* and *tata* with no possessive — like English "Mom" and "Dad". In casual speech there are also merged forms like *frate-meu* and *soră-mea*. Just recognize them; don't use them yet.

blocks.text: Male–female pairs are often formed by adding *-ă*: *bunic → bunică*, like *student → studentă* in unit 1. More distant relatives: *unchi* (uncle), *mătușă* (aunt), *văr* (male cousin), *verișoară* (female cousin), *nepot / nepoată* (nephew / niece; also grandson / granddaughter). A question you'll certainly get: *Ești căsătorit?* to a man, *Ești căsătorită?* to a woman. Budi's answer: *Nu, nu sunt căsătorit.*

blocks.title: Family in Romanian life
items: **La bunici, la țară.** Many city people have grandparents in the countryside, and childhood summer holidays were spent *la bunici* (at the grandparents'), *la țară* (in the countryside). If your colleague vanishes over a long weekend, that's very likely where they went.

**Name days.** Besides birthdays, Romanians celebrate the feast of the saint whose name they carry: all the *Ion*s and *Ioana*s on January 7, the *Maria*s on August 15, the *Andrei*s on November 30. The wish is the same as for a birthday: *La mulți ani!*
**Nași.** Godparents and wedding sponsors (*naș* and *nașă*) are considered family for life — roughly honorary second parents.

blocks.text: Three patterns for the feminine: add **-ă** (*inginer → ingineră*; in *profesor → profesoară* the *o* also widens to *oa*), replace *-tor* with **-toare** (*programator → programatoare*), or add **-iță** (*doctor → doctoriță*). *Medic* is often used as is for women too: *Ea este medic.*

Remember the rule from unit 1: after *a fi*, a job stands **without** *un* or *o* — *Tatăl meu este inginer*, *Sora mea este studentă*. The article only appears when the job has a description: *Este un inginer bun* ("He's a good engineer"). To ask what someone does, learn *Cu ce te ocupi?* whole — politely *Cu ce vă ocupați?* — literally "what do you occupy yourself with?"; verbs like this come in unit 8.
Cover the Romanian column, read the English, and rebuild the sentences from memory.
